newsitem.title: USA: Dole declares he's fighting for America's soul.
newsitem.headline: Dole declares he's fighting for America's soul.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole declared on Friday he was in a battle for the heart and soul of America as President Bill Clinton chipped away at Republican support in the South.
Addressing a rally in Houston, an angry and passionate Dole compared his presidential campaign with his service in the Second World War, when he was badly wounded.
"That was America's future and we prevailed in World War II, and now we're in another fight for the heart and soul of the United States of America," he declared.

The Reuters daily tracking poll showed Dole had lost ground following the disclosure that his campaign manager had made an abortive appeal to Reform Party candidate Ross Perot to drop out of the campaign.

With Election Day 11 days away, Clinton led Dole by 11 percentage points, up from 8.7 points the day before. An ABC poll put Clinton's lead at 12 points and noted Perot's support had inched up to 8 percent.
Perot rebuffed Dole's entreaty, calling it "weird and inconsequential".
An even more telling statistic emerged from a poll in Texas, where Dole held a narrow three-point lead over Clinton in what should be one of the most reliable Republican states in the nation.
The president was expected to return to Texas late next week in his bid to become the first Democrat candidate to carry the Lone Star State in 20 years.
Clinton began the day in Atlanta where he was expected to highlight a proposal to use college students to help teach children to read.

Georgia, home state of House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, was one of four southern states Clinton carried in 1992. He aimed to do better in the region this year and was seen as competitive in at least 10 states.

Dole's speech was a litany of what he said were ethical violations by the Clinton administration, coupled with an angry condemnation of the "liberal media" as well as voters for failing to pay attention.

"We have the president of the United States who won't say he will not pardon somebody who did business with him and might implicate him later on. Where is the outrage in America?" Dole asked, referring to Clinton's refusal to rule out pardons for former Whitewater business partners.

"Where has the media gone in America? ... When will the voters start to focus? ... When do the American people rise up and say, 'Forget the media in America, we're going to make up our minds, you're not going to make up our minds.'"

Going on the attack in Florida on Thursday, Dole admitted publicly that he was frustrated. In Houston he changed his tune a little, saying he was not so much frustrated as puzzled by his inability to convice voters of Clinton's ethical failings.
"I'm not sure I'm frustrated, but I'm a little -- I don't understand," Dole said.
